claim: Malaria caused by the replication of Plasmodium falciparum parasites in red blood cells (RBCs) kills hundreds of thousands of children each year.
source: Malaria caused by the replication of Plasmodium falciparum parasites in red blood cells (RBCs) kills hundreds of thousands of children each year (WHO, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO 2019 report

claim: Parasites must deform RBC membranes to invade them during blood-stage malaria.
source: In each 48-hr cycle of blood-stage malaria, parasites must deform RBC membranes to invade them (Koch, 2017; Kariuki et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to Koch 2017 and Kariuki et al. 2020

claim: Parasites consume hemoglobin and tolerate the resulting oxidative stress during blood-stage malaria.
source: consume hemoglobin and tolerate the resulting oxidative stress (Francis et al., 1997)
evidence: Supported by citation to Francis et al. 1997

claim: Parasites multiply to displace half the RBC volume during blood-stage malaria.
source: multiply to displace half the RBC volume (Hanssen et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to Hanssen et al. 2012

claim: Parasites remodel the RBC membrane to avoid immune detection during blood-stage malaria.
source: remodel the RBC membrane to avoid immune detection (Zhang, 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang 2015

claim: Genetic disorders that alter aspects of RBC biology influence malaria susceptibility.
source: Consequently, genetic disorders that alter aspects of RBC biology are well-known to influence malaria susceptibility (Kwiatkowski, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kwiatkowski 2005

claim: Sickle cell trait impairs parasite growth by altering hemoglobin polymerization at low oxygen tension.
source: For example, sickle cell trait impairs parasite growth by altering hemoglobin polymerization at low oxygen tension (Pasvol et al., 1978; Archer et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to Pasvol et al. 1978 and Archer et al. 2018

claim: G6PD deficiency is thought to make parasitized RBCs more susceptible to breakdown.
source: while deficiency of the G6PD enzyme involved in oxidative stress tolerance is thought to make parasitized RBCs more susceptible to breakdown (Ruwende and Hill, 1998)
evidence: Supported by citation to Ruwende and Hill 1998, with speculative language 'is thought to'

claim: Large genome-wide association studies have identified a few dozen loci that collectively explain up to 11% of the heritability of the risk of severe versus uncomplicated malaria.
source: Large genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified a few dozen loci that collectively explain up to 11% of the heritability of the risk of severe versus uncomplicated malaria (Timmann et al., 2012; Malaria Genomic Epidemiology Network, 2014; Band et al., 2015; Leffler et al., 2017; Ndila et al., 2018; Malaria Genomic Epidemiology Network, 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple GWAS citations

claim: About 10 of the highest-confidence GWAS signals are in or near genes expressed predominantly in RBCs.
source: About 10 of the highest-confidence GWAS signals, including 6 loci known from earlier methods (Allison, 1954; Field et al., 1994; Ruwende and Hill, 1998; Lell et al., 1999; Rowe, 2007; Cao and Galanello, 2010; Galanello and Cao, 2011), are in or near genes expressed predominantly in RBCs.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to GWAS and earlier studies

claim: A GWAS variant has been shown to regulate expression of the ATP2B4 calcium channel.
source: One new GWAS variant has since been shown to regulate expression of the ATP2B4 calcium channel (Zámbó et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Zámbó et al. 2017

claim: A GWAS variant has been associated with RBC dehydration.
source: and to be associated with RBC dehydration (Li et al., 2013b)
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al. 2013b

claim: A functional link between ATP2B4 and P. falciparum replication has yet to be demonstrated.
source: although a functional link between ATP2B4 and P. falciparum replication has yet to be demonstrated
evidence: Statement about absence of evidence

claim: Additional GWAS discoveries of RBC variation important for malaria are not expected without massive increases in sample size.
source: Additional GWAS discoveries of RBC variation important for malaria are not expected without massive increases in sample size (Boyle et al., 2017; Malaria Genomic Epidemiology Network, 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to Boyle et al. 2017 and Malaria Genomic Epidemiology Network 2019

claim: Severe malaria is a complex phenotype that combines many factors from RBCs, the vascular endothelium, the immune system, the parasite, and the environment.
source: in part because of the large number of hypotheses tested. Severe malaria is a complex phenotype that combines many factors from RBCs, the vascular endothelium, the immune system, the parasite, and the environment (Mackinnon et al., 2005; de Mendonça et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mackinnon et al. 2005 and de Mendonça et al. 2012

claim: Heritable RBC phenotypes like mean cell volume, hemoglobin content, and antigenic blood type vary widely within and between human populations.
source: Heritable RBC phenotypes like mean cell volume (MCV), hemoglobin content (HGB/MCH), and antigenic blood type vary widely within and between human populations (Whitfield et al., 1985; Evans et al., 1999; Pilia et al., 2006; Lo et al., 2011; Cooling, 2015; Canela-Xandri et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Large GWAS conducted mostly in Europeans have demonstrated that many blood cell phenotypes are shaped by hundreds of small-effect loci distributed throughout the genome.
source: Large GWAS conducted mostly in Europeans have demonstrated that many blood cell phenotypes are shaped by hundreds of small-effect loci distributed throughout the genome, consistent with polygenic or omnigenic models of complex trait genetics (van der Harst et al., 2012; Astle et al., 2016; Chami et al., 2016; Boyle et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2020; Vuckovic et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple GWAS citations

claim: Certain blood phenotypes like average hemoglobin levels, hematocrit, and RBC membrane fragility differ between African and European populations.
source: Certain blood phenotypes like average hemoglobin levels, hematocrit, and RBC membrane fragility are also known to differ between African and European populations, although the differences are typically small in magnitude (Garn, 1981; Perry et al., 1992; Beutler and West, 2005; Kanias et al., 2017; Page et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Variation in blood phenotypes across populations can largely be explained by a few RBC disease alleles that have been widely selected across Africa for their protective effects on malaria.
source: This variation across populations can largely be explained by a few RBC disease alleles that have been widely selected across Africa for their protective effects on malaria (Beutler and West, 2005; Lo et al., 2011; Kanias et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Beutler and West 2005, Lo et al. 2011, and Kanias et al. 2017

claim: A much larger number of common variants with small individual effects on RBC phenotypes are expected to be globally widespread.
source: Despite the importance of these population-specific variants, a much larger number of common variants with small individual effects on RBC phenotypes are expected to be globally widespread (Biddanda et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Biddanda et al. 2020 and Chen et al. 2020

claim: Blood samples were collected from 121 donors with no known history of blood disorders.
source: We collected blood samples from 121 donors with no known history of blood disorders, most of whom self-identified as having recent African ancestry (Figure 1A).
evidence: Direct statement of study methodology

claim: Most donors self-identified as having recent African ancestry.
source: We collected blood samples from 121 donors with no known history of blood disorders, most of whom self-identified as having recent African ancestry (Figure 1A).
evidence: Direct statement of study methodology

claim: A patient with hereditary elliptocytosis was sampled as a positive control.
source: As a positive control, we also sampled a patient with hereditary elliptocytosis (HE), a polygenic condition characterized by extremely fragile RBC membranes that strongly inhibit P. falciparum growth (Schulman et al., 1990; Facer, 1995; Dhermy et al., 2007; Gallagher, 2013).
evidence: Direct statement of study methodology with citations supporting HE characteristics

claim: Hereditary elliptocytosis is characterized by extremely fragile RBC membranes that strongly inhibit P. falciparum growth.
source: a polygenic condition characterized by extremely fragile RBC membranes that strongly inhibit P. falciparum growth (Schulman et al., 1990; Facer, 1995; Dhermy et al., 2007; Gallagher, 2013)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Whole-exome sequencing was performed on the donors.
source: We performed whole-exome sequencing (Figure 1—source data 1), both to check for the presence of known RBC disease alleles and to confirm the population genetic ancestry of our donors.
evidence: Direct statement of study methodology

claim: Most donors fell along a continuum from African to European ancestry in a principal component analysis.
source: A principal component analysis of more than 35,000 exomic single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) showed that most donors fell along a continuum from African to European ancestry, as defined by data from the 1000 Genomes Project (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 1A

claim: All donors were unrelated, apart from a six-member family.
source: Pairwise kinship coefficients demonstrated that all donors were unrelated, apart from a six-member family with unique ancestry (Figure 1A, light borders).
evidence: Supported by kinship coefficient analysis

claim: 16% of the healthy donors carried pathogenic hemoglobin alleles.
source: We found that 16% of the healthy donors carried pathogenic hemoglobin alleles (Figure 1B), including 5 heterozygotes for hemoglobin S (HbAS), 4 heterozygotes for hemoglobin C (HbAC), and 11 individuals with one or two copies of an HBA2 deletion causing α-thalassemia (Galanello and Cao, 2011).
evidence: Supported by genetic analysis data shown in Figure 1B

claim: 5 donors were heterozygotes for hemoglobin S (HbAS).
source: including 5 heterozygotes for hemoglobin S (HbAS)
evidence: Direct statement of genetic findings

claim: 4 donors were heterozygotes for hemoglobin C (HbAC).
source: 4 heterozygotes for hemoglobin C (HbAC)
evidence: Direct statement of genetic findings

claim: 11 individuals had one or two copies of an HBA2 deletion causing α-thalassemia.
source: and 11 individuals with one or two copies of an HBA2 deletion causing α-thalassemia (Galanello and Cao, 2011)
evidence: Direct statement of genetic findings with citation

claim: 32% of the study population carried at least one G6PD polymorphism associated with G6PD deficiency.
source: We also scored eight polymorphisms in G6PD that have been functionally associated with various degrees of G6PD deficiency (Yoshida et al., 1971; Clarke et al., 2017) and found that 32% of the study population carried at least one, including 12 of the 20 donors with hemoglobinopathies.
evidence: Direct statement of genetic findings with citations

claim: 12 of the 20 donors with hemoglobinopathies also carried G6PD polymorphisms.
source: including 12 of the 20 donors with hemoglobinopathies
evidence: Direct statement of genetic findings

claim: Among those with wild-type hemoglobin, 1 individual had polymorphisms associated with severe G6PD deficiency.
source: Among those with wild-type hemoglobin, we identified 1 individual with polymorphisms associated with severe G6PD deficiency (>60% loss of function)
evidence: Direct statement of genetic findings

claim: Among those with wild-type hemoglobin, 23 individuals had polymorphisms associated with mild to medium G6PD deficiency.
source: and 23 with polymorphisms associated with mild to medium deficiency (<42% loss of function)
evidence: Direct statement of genetic findings

claim: No alleles linked to other monogenic RBC disorders, including β-thalassemia or xerocytosis, were detected.
source: We detected no alleles linked to other monogenic RBC disorders, including β-thalassemia or xerocytosis (Cao and Galanello, 2010; Glogowska et al., 2017).
evidence: Direct statement of genetic findings with citations

claim: 68 unrelated donors were classified as 'non-carriers' of known disease alleles.
source: We therefore classified the remaining 68 unrelated donors as 'non-carriers' of known disease alleles for the purposes of this work.
evidence: Direct statement of study classification

claim: P. falciparum growth rates ranged from 64% to 136% for 3D7 among non-carriers.
source: Among non-carriers, growth rates ranged from 64% to 136% for 3D7 (SD=17.7%)
evidence: Direct statement of experimental results

claim: P. falciparum growth rates ranged from 76% to 128% for Th.026.09 among non-carriers.
source: and 76% to 128% for Th.026.09 (SD=10.6%) (Figure 2A–B)
evidence: Direct statement of experimental results shown in Figure 2A-B

claim: Per-sample growth rates were strongly correlated between the two P. falciparum strains.
source: Per-sample growth rates were strongly correlated between the two strains (Figure 2C, R2=0.69, p<3×10–16)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2C

claim: Growth rates were positively correlated when measured in different weeks.
source: and positively correlated when measured in different weeks (p=0.35, Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Reductions in mean growth rate were detected for both strains in RBCs carrying known disease alleles.
source: Furthermore, as expected (Friedman, 1978; Ifediba et al., 1985; Greene, 1993; Facer, 1995), we detected reductions in mean growth rate for both strains in RBCs carrying known disease alleles.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to prior work

claim: α-thalassemia trait was associated with reduced P. falciparum growth for 3D7 (p=0.027).
source: These included individuals with α-thalassemia trait (3D7 p=0.027; Th.026.09 p=0.077)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: HbAS was associated with reduced P. falciparum growth for both strains.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The wide distribution of growth rates for non-carrier RBCs had considerable overlap with the growth rates in carrier RBCs.
source: Notably, the wide distribution of growth rates for non-carrier RBCs had considerable overlap with the growth rates in carrier RBCs.
evidence: Inference from experimental data

claim: Only the HbAS and HE samples fell entirely outside the non-carrier range for growth rates.
source: Only the HbAS and HE samples fell entirely outside the non-carrier range.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental observation

claim: Previously unknown RBC variation exists that impacts P. falciparum growth with cumulative effect sizes comparable to known disease alleles.
source: This observation implies the existence of previously unknown RBC variation that impacts P. falciparum growth, which may have cumulative effect sizes comparable to known disease alleles.
evidence: Inference from the overlap of non-carrier and carrier distributions

claim: P. falciparum invasion rates ranged from 70% to 143% for 3D7 among non-carriers.
source: Among non-carriers, invasion rates ranged from 70% to 143% for 3D7 (SD=14.9%)
evidence: Direct statement of experimental results

claim: P. falciparum invasion rates ranged from 41% to 193% for Th.026.09 among non-carriers.
source: and 41% to 193% for Th.026.09 (SD=29.1%) (Figure 2D–E)
evidence: Direct statement of experimental results shown in Figure 2D-E

claim: HbAC was associated with an 11% decrease in 3D7 invasion (p=0.008).
source: HbAC was associated with an 11% decrease in 3D7 invasion (p=0.008)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: α-thalassemia trait was associated with a 22% increase in Th.026.09 invasion (p=0.091).
source: while α-thalassemia trait was associated with a 22% increase in Th.026.09 invasion (p=0.091)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: HE had a strong effect on the invasion efficiency of both strains.
source: Only HE had a strong effect on the invasion efficiency of both strains.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental observation

claim: The correlation of invasion efficiencies between strains was weaker than for growth.
source: The correlation of invasion efficiencies between strains was weaker than for growth (Figure 2F, R2=0.10, p=6×10–4)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2F

claim: Greater batch effects were observed for invasion than for growth.
source: However, we also observed greater batch effects (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and greater variability between repeated samples (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) for invasion than for growth
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2

claim: Invasion is influenced by greater experimental noise than growth.
source: suggesting that invasion is influenced by greater experimental noise
evidence: Inference from batch effects and variability data

claim: HbAC was associated with elevated CHCM (p=0.033), consistent with dehydration.
source: These included elevated CHCM for HbAC (p=0.033), consistent with dehydration
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: α-thalassemia trait (−α/−α) was associated with very low MCV (p=6.8×10–5) and MCH (p=2.5×10–7), consistent with microcytic anemia.
source: and very low MCV (p=6.8×10–5) and MCH (p=2.5×10–7) for α-thalassemia trait (−α/−α), consistent with microcytic anemia (Galanello and Cao, 2011)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and citation

claim: RBCs from the HE patient had very low MCV and MCH, reflecting membrane breakage and volume loss.
source: RBCs from the HE patient also had very low MCV and MCH, reflecting the membrane breakage and volume loss characteristic of this disease.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and established knowledge of HE

claim: Broad distributions in non-carriers overlapped the distributions of most carriers for all phenotypic measures.
source: For all these phenotypic measures, we also observed broad distributions in non-carriers that overlapped the distributions of most carriers (Figure 3A–D; Figure 3—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3 and supplements

claim: The breadth of the non-carrier distribution for each phenotype was large compared to the average difference between Africans and Europeans.
source: Notably, the breadth of the non-carrier distribution for each phenotype was large (e.g., 24 fl range for MCV) compared to the average difference between Africans and Europeans (e.g., 3–5 fl; Beutler and West, 2005; Lo et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations

claim: Healthy RBCs exist on the same phenotypic continuum as RBCs carrying known disease alleles.
source: This wide diversity and substantial overlap between non-carrier and carrier traits suggest that healthy RBCs exist on the same phenotypic continuum as RBCs carrying known disease alleles.
evidence: Inference from the overlap of distributions

claim: Specific hemoglobinopathies were associated with moderate to strong reductions in fragility, deformability, and/or resistance to loss of deformability when dehydrated.
source: Specific hemoglobinopathies were associated with moderate to strong reductions in fragility, deformability, and/or resistance to loss of deformability when dehydrated (Figure 3—figure supplements 3–5).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 3-5

claim: HE cells were both extremely fragile and extremely non-deformable.
source: HE cells were both extremely fragile and extremely non-deformable.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental observation

claim: The distributions for all membrane measures in non-carriers were wide, continuous, and overlapped the distribution of most carriers.
source: In non-carriers, the distributions for all membrane measures were wide, continuous, and overlapped the distribution of most carriers (Figure 3E–H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3E-H

claim: Multiple phenotypic alterations associated with RBC disease alleles are also present in non-carrier RBCs.
source: Overall, these data demonstrate that multiple phenotypic alterations associated with RBC disease alleles are also present in non-carrier RBCs.
evidence: Summary inference from experimental data

claim: Ohyper was the most strongly predictive phenotype for P. falciparum fitness in non-carrier RBCs.
source: Among 25 tested phenotypes, the most strongly predictive was the ektacytometry parameter Ohyper, which represents a cell's tendency to retain deformability in the face of dehydration (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by LASSO analysis results

claim: Non-carrier RBCs with the largest Ohyper values supported 22–46% faster parasite growth than RBCs with the smallest Ohyper values.
source: In univariate models, non-carrier RBCs with the largest Ohyper values—that is, those that retained more deformability when dehydrated—supported 22–46% faster parasite growth (3D7 p=0.003, Th.026.09 p=0.007)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Non-carrier RBCs with the largest Ohyper values supported 31–83% more effective invasion than RBCs with the smallest Ohyper values.
source: and 31–83% more effective invasion (3D7 p=0.008, Th.026.09 p=0.005) than RBCs with the smallest Ohyper values, which quickly lost deformability
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: P. falciparum replication was inhibited in RBCs that were more dehydrated at baseline.
source: Consistent with this result, P. falciparum replication was inhibited in RBCs that were more dehydrated at baseline (e.g., with higher CHCM; 3D7 invasion p=0.006, 3D7 growth p=0.024, Th.026.09 invasion p=0.004, Th.026.09 growth p=0.26).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Parasites grew faster in RBCs with larger mean volume (MCV).
source: Parasites also grew faster in RBCs with larger mean volume (MCV; 3D7 p=0.001, Th.026.09 p=0.0009)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Parasites grew faster in RBCs with a greater mass of hemoglobin per cell (MCH).
source: a greater mass of hemoglobin per cell (MCH; 3D7 p=0.071, Th.026.09 p=0.016)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Parasites grew faster in RBCs with more deformable membranes (DImax).
source: and more deformable membranes (DImax; 3D7 p=0.0005, Th.026.09 p=0.008)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: 3D7 growth was reduced in RBCs with more fragile membranes (O50; p=0.005).
source: 3D7 growth was also reduced in RBCs with more fragile membranes (O50; p=0.005).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Common, non-pathogenic variation in RBC size, membrane dynamics, and other correlated traits have meaningful effects on P. falciparum replication rate in RBCs.
source: These results indicate that common, non-pathogenic variation in RBC size, membrane dynamics, and other correlated traits have meaningful effects on P. falciparum replication rate in RBCs.
evidence: Summary inference from experimental data

claim: Non-carrier phenotypes selected by LASSO explained 3–9% of the variation in parasite growth in test data.
source: Taken together, the non-carrier phenotypes selected by LASSO from training data (N~61, Figure 4A) explained 3–9% of the variation in parasite growth in separate test data (N~7, Figure 4B; 3D7 p=0.008 and RMSE=18.0%; Th.026.09 p=0.079 and RMSE=10.8%).
evidence: Supported by LASSO cross-validation analysis shown in Figure 4B

claim: The variance explained by phenotypes was significantly greater than expected from random permutations.
source: This fraction was significantly greater than expected from random permutations, which were centered on R2=0 in the test data (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by permutation analysis shown in Figure 4B

claim: Prediction error was greater for individuals with parasite growth values farther away from the mean.
source: Notably, prediction error was greater for individuals with parasite growth values farther away from the mean.
evidence: Observation from LASSO analysis

claim: For invasion, RBC phenotypes did not explain more variation in the test data than expected from permutations.
source: In contrast, for invasion, RBC phenotypes did not explain more variation in the test data than expected from permutations (Figure 4C; 3D7 p=0.79 and RMSE=15.0%; Th.026.09 p=0.53 and RMSE=29.5%).
evidence: Supported by LASSO cross-validation analysis shown in Figure 4C

claim: All phenotype models were less predictive for the clinical isolate Th.026.09 than the lab strain 3D7.
source: All phenotype models were less predictive for the clinical isolate Th.026.09 than the lab strain 3D7, perhaps because clinical isolates are less adapted to laboratory conditions.
evidence: Observation from LASSO analysis with speculative explanation

claim: Non-carrier cells that are less hospitable to parasites share specific traits with RBCs that carry disease alleles, including smaller size, decreased deformability, and an increased tendency to lose deformability when dehydrating.
source: Overall, these results demonstrate that multiple, variable phenotypes impact P. falciparum susceptibility in healthy RBCs. Non-carrier cells that are less hospitable to parasites share specific traits with RBCs that carry disease alleles, including smaller size, decreased deformability, and an increased tendency to lose deformability when dehydrating.
evidence: Summary inference from experimental data

claim: Genotypes and phenotypes selected by LASSO explained 7–15% of the variation in parasite growth rate in the test data.
source: Taken together, genotypes and phenotypes selected by LASSO explained 7–15% of the variation in parasite growth rate in the test data (Figure 5B; 3D7 p=0.012 and RMSE=16.5%; Th.026.09 p=0.063 and RMSE=10.6%).
evidence: Supported by LASSO cross-validation analysis shown in Figure 5B

claim: The variance explained by models using real genotype and phenotype data was significantly larger than expected from permutation and random sets of RBC genes.
source: The variance explained by models using real genotype and phenotype data was significantly larger than expected from permutation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and random sets of RBC genes (Figure 5B), suggesting that the 23 malaria-related genes contain variation that influences P. falciparum development.
evidence: Supported by permutation and random gene set analyses

claim: The 23 malaria-related genes contain variation that influences P. falciparum development.
source: suggesting that the 23 malaria-related genes contain variation that influences P. falciparum development
evidence: Inference from LASSO analysis comparing real genes to random gene sets

claim: Nearly all of the 32 polymorphisms selected by LASSO in growth models occurred in ion channel proteins, components of the flexible RBC membrane backbone, or red cell plasma membrane proteins.
source: Nearly all of the 32 polymorphisms selected by LASSO in growth models occurred in (1) ion channel proteins, which regulate RBC hydration; (2) components of the flexible RBC membrane backbone; or (3) red cell plasma membrane proteins, including known invasion receptors (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by LASSO analysis results shown in Figure 5A

claim: PIEZO1 contained seven polymorphisms associated with small to moderate reductions of P. falciparum growth rate.
source: In the first category, the highly polymorphic ion channel PIEZO1 contained seven polymorphisms associated with small (<3.7%) to moderate (31%) reductions of P. falciparum growth rate.
evidence: Supported by LASSO analysis results

claim: PIEZO1-E756del predicted a moderate reduction in Th.026.09 growth (–7.9%, p=0.01).
source: The microsatellite variant PIEZO1-E756del, which has been a focus of several recent studies (Ilboudo et al., 2018; Ma et al., 2018; Rooks et al., 2019; Nguetse et al., 2020), predicted a moderate reduction in Th.026.09 growth (–7.9%, p=0.01)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and citations

claim: PIEZO1-E756del was not related to RBC dehydration in these data.
source: but was not related to RBC dehydration in these data (Figure 5—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2

claim: One growth-associated variant in ATP2B4 was detected for 3D7 (–5.9%, p=0.075).
source: For 3D7, we also detected one growth-associated variant in ATP2B4 (–5.9%, p=0.075), which encodes the primary RBC calcium channel PMCA4b.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: The ATP2B4 variant tags a haplotype implicated by GWAS in protection from severe malaria and many RBC phenotypes.
source: This variant tags an ATP2B4 haplotype implicated by GWAS in protection from severe malaria and many RBC phenotypes (van der Harst et al., 2012; Li et al., 2013b; Lessard et al., 2017; Lin et al., 2020, Timmann et al., 2012, Zámbó et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple GWAS citations

claim: The ATP2B4 variant has never before been functionally demonstrated to be associated with P. falciparum fitness.
source: Notably, however, this variant has never before been functionally demonstrated to be associated with P. falciparum fitness.
evidence: Statement about novelty of finding

claim: SPTA1 and SPTB contained several variants associated with the growth of at least one P. falciparum strain.
source: SPTA1 and SPTB, which encode the flexible spectrin backbone of RBCs, contained several variants associated with the growth of at least one P. falciparum strain, as did the structural linker genes ANK1, SLC4A1, and EPB42 (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by LASSO analysis results shown in Figure 5A

claim: 10 polymorphisms in ABCB6, GYPB, GYPC, CR1, CD44, and basigin (BSG) were associated with P. falciparum growth.
source: We also identified a total of 10 polymorphisms in ABCB6, GYPB, GYPC, CR1, CD44, and basigin (BSG) that were associated with P. falciparum growth.
evidence: Supported by LASSO analysis results

claim: These plasma membrane proteins have all been previously implicated in P. falciparum invasion by genetic deficiency studies.
source: These plasma membrane proteins have all been previously implicated in P. falciparum invasion by genetic deficiency studies (Mayer et al., 2009; Crosnier et al., 2011; Egan et al., 2015; Egan et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Two of the variants identified are synonymous quantitative trait loci (QTL) for CD44 splicing (rs35356320) and BSG expression (rs4682).
source: Notably, two of the variants identified here are synonymous quantitative trait loci (QTL) for CD44 splicing (rs35356320) and BSG expression (rs4682) (GTEx Consortium et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to GTEx Consortium et al. 2017

claim: No associated variants were detected in 10 tested genes including hemoglobin proteins, G6PD, glycophorins, CD55, EPB41, FPN, and HP.
source: No associated variants were detected in the other 10 tested genes, including 3 hemoglobin proteins, G6PD, 2 glycophorins, CD55, EPB41, FPN, and HP.
evidence: Direct statement of analysis results

claim: Dozens of host genetic variants shape the phenotypic distribution of red cell susceptibility to P. falciparum in non-carriers.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that dozens of host genetic variants shape the phenotypic distribution of red cell susceptibility to P. falciparum in non-carriers.
evidence: Summary inference from genetic analysis

claim: 18 of the 32 variants selected by LASSO were synonymous.
source: Eighteen of the 32 variants selected by LASSO were synonymous, which was not significantly different from the input set of 106 variants (p=0.72, two-sided binomial test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis

claim: Over half of the growth-associated variants have previously been associated with gene expression traits, GWAS traits, or GWAS loci through linkage.
source: Over half of the growth-associated variants have previously been associated with gene expression traits, GWAS traits, or GWAS loci through linkage (Figure 5—source data 3), suggesting that they indeed tag functional polymorphisms.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 5—source data 3

claim: Novel variants contribute substantially to the predictive power of these models.
source: Novel variants nonetheless contribute substantially to the predictive power of these models (Figure 5—figure supplement 4)
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4

claim: Nearly all the variants are novel in terms of association with P. falciparum growth rate.
source: and nearly all the variants are novel in terms of association with P. falciparum growth rate
evidence: Statement about novelty of findings

claim: Models of invasion that included genotypic predictors were no more accurate than expected by chance.
source: In contrast to growth, models of invasion that included genotypic predictors were no more accurate than expected by chance (Figure 5C, p≥0.3; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, p≥0.15).
evidence: Supported by LASSO cross-validation analysis

claim: Six of the nine RBC invasion receptors contained variants associated with growth.
source: However, six of the nine RBC invasion receptors contained variants associated with growth (Figure 5A)
evidence: Supported by LASSO analysis results shown in Figure 5A

claim: A SNP in glycophorin B (GYPB) has been linked to malaria risk in Brazil.
source: including a SNP in glycophorin B (GYPB) that has been linked to malaria risk in Brazil (Tarazona-Santos et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to Tarazona-Santos et al. 2011

claim: No PCs of population structure were significantly associated with P. falciparum growth rate.
source: No PCs of population structure were significantly associated with P. falciparum growth rate (Figure 5—source data 3), including the PC that distinguishes Africans from other populations (PC1, Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis

claim: One PC was selected by LASSO for 3D7 growth, but this association was driven by a single donor with East Asian ancestry.
source: One PC was selected by LASSO for 3D7 growth, but this association was driven by a single donor with East Asian ancestry and relatively high susceptibility (Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5

claim: No evidence was found that African ancestry predicts P. falciparum resistance in non-carrier RBCs, apart from a positive relationship between African ancestry and invasion rate of Th.026.09.
source: Surprisingly, we found no evidence that these traits were related, apart from a positive relationship between African ancestry and invasion rate of Th.026.09, the clinical Senegalese strain (p=0.004, R2=0.13, Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6D

claim: Greater African ancestry predicts reduced osmotic fragility (p=1.2×10–6).
source: We found that greater African ancestry predicts reduced osmotic fragility (p=1.2×10–6)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis

claim: Greater African ancestry predicts reduced RBC dehydration (CHCM p=0.009; MCHC p=0.089).
source: reduced RBC dehydration (CHCM p=0.009; MCHC p=0.089)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis

claim: Greater African ancestry predicts a greater fraction of 'overhydrated' RBCs with normal volume and low hemoglobin (M4 p=0.041).
source: and a greater fraction of 'overhydrated' RBCs with normal volume and low hemoglobin (M4 p=0.041)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis

claim: All of these traits associated with African ancestry actually predict greater red cell susceptibility to P. falciparum.
source: All of these traits actually predict greater red cell susceptibility to P. falciparum (Figure 4A)
evidence: Inference from combining results from Figure 4A and ancestry analysis

claim: 11 of 22 protective alleles (50%) are more common in Africans, which is not more than expected by chance (p=0.5).
source: We found that 11 of these protective alleles (50%) are more common in Africans, which is not more than expected by chance (p=0.5, one-sided binomial test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of allele frequencies

claim: The three protective variants with the largest absolute FST values are all more common in Europeans.
source: The three protective variants with the largest absolute FST values are all more common in Europeans, including a synonymous SPTA1 allele with GWAS associations to several RBC and white blood cell traits.
evidence: Supported by FST analysis

claim: Two protective PIEZO1 variants are more common in Africans, including E756del and a synonymous variant of large effect.
source: Two protective PIEZO1 variants are more common in Africans, including E756del and a synonymous variant of large effect.
evidence: Supported by FST analysis

claim: There is no evidence that African populations are enriched for non-pathogenic RBC polymorphisms or phenotypes associated with impaired P. falciparum growth in vitro.
source: Overall, however, we find no evidence that African populations are enriched for non-pathogenic RBC polymorphisms or phenotypes associated with impaired P. falciparum growth in vitro.
evidence: Summary inference from ancestry and allele frequency analyses

claim: Exponential replication of P. falciparum is a significant driver of malaria disease progression.
source: Exponential replication of P. falciparum is a significant driver of malaria disease progression (Bejon et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bejon et al. 2007

claim: Growth inhibition from HbAS reduces the risk of death from malaria by reducing parasite density in the blood.
source: Growth inhibition from HbAS, for example, reduces the risk of death from malaria by reducing parasite density in the blood (Allison, 1954; Luzzatto, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Allison 1954 and Luzzatto 2012

claim: A threefold range of parasite replication rates was found among non-carrier RBCs that share substantial overlap with RBCs carrying other protective variants.
source: While HbAS has a uniquely extreme effect size, we found a threefold range of parasite replication rates among non-carrier RBCs that share substantial overlap with RBCs carrying other protective variants.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: Widespread, 'normal' variation in RBC hydration and deformability traits are associated with P. falciparum fitness in non-carrier RBCs.
source: We have shown here that widespread, 'normal' variation in RBC hydration and deformability traits are associated with P. falciparum fitness in non-carrier RBCs.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: The protective phenotypes detected in non-carrier RBCs are also present in carriers, albeit to a stronger degree.
source: Interestingly, the protective phenotypes we detect in non-carrier RBCs are also present in carriers, albeit to a stronger degree (Clark et al., 1983; Mockenhaupt, 2000; Pengon et al., 2018).
evidence: Inference from experimental data with citations

claim: Chemical or genetic dehydration of RBCs reduces P. falciparum growth.
source: These results are consistent with experimental manipulations that reduce P. falciparum growth, such as chemical or genetic dehydration of RBCs (Tiffert et al., 2005; Ma et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tiffert et al. 2005 and Ma et al. 2018

claim: Dantu, a rare glycophorin variant associated with increased membrane tension, confers a protective effect.
source: They are also consistent with the protective effect conferred by Dantu, a rare glycophorin variant associated with increased membrane tension (Field et al., 1994; Leffler et al., 2017; Kariuki et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Field et al. 1994, Leffler et al. 2017, and Kariuki et al. 2020

claim: Common, healthy phenotypic variation in RBC traits contributes meaningfully to P. falciparum growth.
source: Our data expand upon these prior findings by demonstrating for the first time that common, healthy phenotypic variation in RBC traits contributes meaningfully to P. falciparum growth.
evidence: Summary inference from experimental data

claim: The broad distribution of RBC phenotypes in humans is shaped by a large number of common alleles.
source: These studies agree that the broad distribution of RBC phenotypes in humans is shaped by a large number of common alleles, similar to other complex traits (Boyle et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Boyle et al. 2017 and reference to GWAS studies

claim: Different combinations of alleles may underlie the broad phenotypic variation observed in non-carriers.
source: Although the effects of most individual alleles are likely too small to be considered pathogenic on their own, different combinations of alleles may underlie the broad phenotypic variation observed in non-carriers.
evidence: Inference from genetic architecture of complex traits

claim: Some RBC phenotypes are shaped by environmental variation, such as diet and time of day.
source: Some RBC phenotypes are also shaped by environmental variation, such as diet and time of day (England et al., 1976; Sennels et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to England et al. 1976 and Sennels et al. 2011

claim: Genetic variation in a small number of RBC proteins outperformed phenotypic variation in linear models of P. falciparum growth.
source: In our linear models of P. falciparum growth, phenotypic variation among RBCs was outperformed by genetic variation in a small number of RBC proteins.
evidence: Summary of LASSO analysis results

claim: Protective RBC phenotypes exist that were not measured or not measured with sufficient accuracy.
source: This result implies the existence of protective RBC phenotypes that we did not measure (or did not measure with sufficient accuracy), such as quantitative proteomic, transcriptomic, and metabolomic traits that could be addressed by future studies.
evidence: Inference from model performance

claim: Silent and coding SNPs are equally likely to be associated with human disease.
source: Indeed, silent and coding SNPs are equally likely to be associated with human disease (Chen et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al. 2010

claim: Many synonymous sites experience strong selection.
source: and many synonymous sites experience strong selection (Supek et al., 2014; Machado et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to Supek et al. 2014 and Machado et al. 2020

claim: The true number of RBC phenotypes that impact P. falciparum may be effectively infinite.
source: The true number of RBC phenotypes that impact P. falciparum may be effectively infinite (Kinsler et al., 2020)
evidence: Speculative statement with citation to Kinsler et al. 2020

claim: Focusing tests on a limited number of hypotheses helps ensure that 'significant' results are reliable.
source: However, testing fewer hypotheses that are more likely to be true helps ensure that 'significant' results are reliable (Ioannidis, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ioannidis 2005

claim: Future studies with many more than 68 non-carriers will be required to discover additional associations in unknown genes, non-genic regulatory variation, and any alleles with smaller effects.
source: However, future studies with many more than 68 non-carriers will be required to discover additional associations in unknown genes, non-genic regulatory variation, and any alleles with smaller effects.
evidence: Inference about study limitations and future directions

claim: Genetic linkage complicates the identification of the exact functional polymorphisms in any population sample.
source: It is also important to note that genetic linkage complicates the identification of the exact functional polymorphisms in any population sample (Sohail et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to Sohail et al. 2019

claim: About half of the associated variants occur in linkage blocks containing other SNPs associated with RBC traits by GWAS.
source: Indeed, about half of our associated variants occur in linkage blocks containing other SNPs associated with RBC traits by GWAS.
evidence: Statement about linkage analysis

claim: The evidence most strongly supports the conclusion that 13 specific RBC genes are strongly enriched for polymorphisms with impacts on P. falciparum growth.
source: In this way, our evidence most strongly supports the conclusion that 13 specific RBC genes are strongly enriched for polymorphisms with impacts on P. falciparum growth.
evidence: Summary inference from genetic analysis

claim: The associations observed for parasite growth were stronger and more significant than the associations for parasite invasion.
source: The associations we observed for parasite growth were stronger and more significant than the associations for parasite invasion.
evidence: Summary of analysis results

claim: Batch effects played a role in the weaker invasion associations.
source: While batch effects clearly played a role
evidence: Inference from experimental observations

claim: Missing invasion data in 10 non-carrier samples reduced statistical power.
source: this may also be due to missing invasion data in 10 non-carrier samples (see Materials and methods) that reduced statistical power
evidence: Statement about study limitations

claim: The 'growth' measurement includes a 're-invasion' event.
source: The invasion data also allow us to highlight unique and interesting trends in the Senegalese clinical strain and in carriers of hemoglobin C. We also observed weaker associations for the clinical strain Th.026.09 than for the lab strain 3D7.
evidence: Statement about experimental design

claim: 3D7 and Th.026.09 display large differences in absolute growth rate.
source: These strains display large differences in absolute growth rate, possibly because Th.026.09 carries costly alleles for drug resistance and 3D7 has had decades longer to adapt to lab conditions (Walliker et al., 1987; Daniels et al., 2012; Moser, 2020).
evidence: Observation with speculative explanation and citations

claim: African ancestry predicted higher invasion only for Th.026.09, which might indicate that this strain is better adapted to African RBCs.
source: Interestingly, African ancestry predicted higher invasion only for Th.026.09, which might indicate that this strain is better adapted to African RBCs.
evidence: Observation with speculative interpretation

claim: Normalized fitness values were significantly correlated between the two strains across donors.
source: Despite these differences, we showed that normalized fitness values were significantly correlated between the two strains across donors.
evidence: Summary of statistical analysis

claim: Several RBC phenotypes and genotypes that predicted fitness in one strain were also replicated in the other.
source: Several RBC phenotypes and genotypes that predicted fitness in one strain were also replicated in the other.
evidence: Summary of analysis results

claim: The findings may be generalizable across divergent strains of P. falciparum.
source: These results suggest that our findings may be generalizable across divergent strains of P. falciparum, although future studies would benefit by testing many more lab strains and clinical isolates.
evidence: Inference from strain comparison with caveat

claim: A recent test of data from a large GWAS for severe malaria was unable to demonstrate that natural selection has driven many malaria-protective alleles to higher frequencies in African versus European populations.
source: Notably, a recent test of data from a large GWAS for severe malaria (Malaria Genomic Epidemiology Network, 2019) was also unable to demonstrate that natural selection has driven many malaria-protective alleles to higher frequencies in African versus European populations.
evidence: Supported by citation to Malaria Genomic Epidemiology Network 2019

claim: The majority of non-pathogenic variants may not have had sufficient time to increase in frequency since P. falciparum began expanding in humans some 5000–10,000 years ago.
source: First, compared to large-effect disease alleles, the majority of non-pathogenic variants may not have had sufficient time to increase in frequency since P. falciparum began expanding in humans some 5000–10,000 years ago (Sundararaman et al., 2016; Otto et al., 2018).
evidence: Speculative explanation with citations

claim: The complexity of severe malaria could mean that the variants discovered here do not substantially impact disease outcome.
source: Second, the complexity of severe malaria could mean that the variants discovered here do not substantially impact disease outcome, especially relative to known disease variants.
evidence: Speculative explanation

claim: The variants discovered here may have pleiotropic effects on other phenotypes, which are themselves subject to other selective pressures besides malaria resistance.
source: Third, the variants discovered here may have pleiotropic effects on other phenotypes, which are themselves subject to other selective pressures besides malaria resistance.
evidence: Speculative explanation

claim: Human adaptation may be too local to detect with coarse-grain sampling of sub-Saharan African genetic diversity.
source: Finally, human adaptation may be too local to detect with coarse-grain sampling of sub-Saharan African genetic diversity (e.g., Pankratov et al., 2020).
evidence: Speculative explanation with citation

claim: Few RBC alleles remain to be discovered that are both particularly common in Africa and have large effects on P. falciparum proliferation in RBCs.
source: Overall, however, our data suggest that few RBC alleles remain to be discovered that are both particularly common in Africa and have large effects on P. falciparum proliferation in RBCs.
evidence: Summary inference from ancestry and allele frequency analyses

claim: It may be inaccurate to make assumptions about RBC susceptibility to P. falciparum based on a person's race or continental ancestry.
source: More broadly, these data show that it may be inaccurate to make assumptions about RBC susceptibility to P. falciparum based on a person's race or continental ancestry.
evidence: Inference from ancestry analysis results

claim: >90% of the total genetic variation among humans occurs within populations, rather than across them.
source: This result is an important reminder that >90% of the total genetic variation among humans occurs within populations, rather than across them (Lewontin, 1972; Rosenberg, 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to Lewontin 1972 and Rosenberg 2011

claim: The majority of common genetic variation is shared among all human populations.
source: and that the majority of common genetic variation is shared among all human populations (Biddanda et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to Biddanda et al. 2020

claim: Substantial phenotypic and genetic diversity in healthy human RBCs impacts the replication of malaria parasites.
source: In conclusion, this study demonstrates that substantial phenotypic and genetic diversity in healthy human RBCs impacts the replication of malaria parasites.
evidence: Summary of study findings

claim: A better understanding of how P. falciparum biology is impacted by natural RBC variation could help lead to new therapies for malaria.
source: Whether or not this diversity is shaped by malaria selection, a better understanding of how P. falciparum biology is impacted by natural RBC variation could help lead to new therapies for one of humanity's most important infectious diseases.
evidence: Speculative statement about future applications

claim: Over one-third of healthy donors unknowingly carried alleles for G6PD deficiency or hemoglobinopathies.
source: Over one-third of healthy donors unknowingly carried alleles for G6PD deficiency or hemoglobinopathies, which were associated with characteristic RBC phenotypes.
evidence: Summary of genetic findings from the study

claim: Among non-carriers alone, variation in RBC hydration, membrane deformability, and volume was strongly associated with P. falciparum growth rate.
source: Among non-carriers alone, variation in RBC hydration, membrane deformability, and volume was strongly associated with P. falciparum growth rate.
evidence: Summary of phenotypic association findings

claim: Common genetic variants in PIEZO1, SPTA1/SPTB, and several P. falciparum invasion receptors were associated with parasite growth rate.
source: Common genetic variants in PIEZO1, SPTA1/SPTB, and several P. falciparum invasion receptors were also associated with parasite growth rate.
evidence: Summary of genetic association findings

claim: Little or negative evidence was observed for divergent selection on non-pathogenic RBC variation between Africans and Europeans.
source: Interestingly, we observed little or negative evidence for divergent selection on non-pathogenic RBC variation between Africans and Europeans.
evidence: Summary of ancestry analysis findings

claim: Globally widespread variation in a moderate number of genes and phenotypes modulates P. falciparum fitness in RBCs.
source: These findings suggest a model in which globally widespread variation in a moderate number of genes and phenotypes modulates P. falciparum fitness in RBCs.
evidence: Summary inference from all study findings
